title: TA8-06118
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons I reject the refugee claim of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a 30 year old citizen of Colombia. Allegations

The claimant alleges that her family was active in a human rights organization, XXXXX XXXXX, in the XXXXX area. The claimant believes that even though she was not a member since she did volunteer work, she is at risk of harm from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia - People's Army (FARC) and the United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia, AUC) should she return to Colombia today.
In addition she asserts her father was a XXXXX targeted by FARC. It is her belief that this fact would also put her at risk. Determination

I found the claimant was not a credible witness and on this basis reject her claim. In addition I am satisfied that Bogota is a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) and the claimant failed to establish that state protection for her in Bogota would be inadequate. Analysis

Originally this claim was joined to that of her husband, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. When that relationship dissolved the claimant asked that her claim be disjoined from that of her husband. The Board granted the application.
Were the claimant's actions prior to coming to Canada in 2008 consistent with her fear of being seriously harmed in Colombia? I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities this is not the case.
According to the revised narrative1 the claimant was sent to Canada in 1998 to protect her from the danger faced by the family and for her to learn English.
While in Canada her parents fled Colombia to the United States (U.S.) because of the threats they were receiving.
The claimant went to the U.S. from Canada and after visiting her mother the claimant returned to Colombia to continue her studies. At this time the claimant was 19 years old.
When she returned to the U.S. in XXXXX 2000 she explained she did not make a claim for asylum since her parents had not claimed.

However if the rest of the family fled Colombia fearing harm and had sent the claimant to Canada fearing she would be harmed, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities the family would have insisted their 19 year old daughter stay in the U.S. and go to school there. She states she returned to Colombia against her parents' wishes. I do not accept this is likely. She returned to XXXXX, the area of Colombia from which her parents fled. It is implausible that if her parents fled XXXXX due to a fear of FARC that the claimant would return to the same area only one year later.
After returning to the U.S. fearful of persecution in Colombia, the claimant lived without status for approximately six years after her student visa expired.

She explained she married a U.S. citizen who started a sponsorship process but when the marriage ended that process stopped. In addition her family was informed by a lawyer that they could not make a claim after one year, however, the claimant never sought independent legal advice even after the marriage dissolved.

In addition in 2004 the claimant made three trips back to Colombia to XXXXX where she believes FARC was interested in she and her family in the past. She explained she visited her grandmother who was very ill and did not go out much. In addition the visits were of short durations.

Even so she entered Colombia through the XXXXX airport. Today she believes she would be found due to the intelligence network of FARC. If that is the case, then returning to Colombia on three occasions through the very airport where FARC might be looking for her, I find is inconsistent with her fears and understanding as to the capability of FARC. When I consider -
First, the claimant returned to XXXXX, Colombia from Canada and the U.S. to study after her family had fled, fearful for their lives.
Second, the claimant returned to XXXXX, Colombia on three more occasions after she believed family members had been murdered by FARC.

The claimant did not make a claim for asylum in 1999 before returning to Colombia, or in XXXXX 2000 after returning to the U.S. when she believed she was at further risk of harm in Colombia, or in 2004 after being in Colombia on three occasions, or when her marriage to a U.S. citizen failed. Finally, the total time in the U.S. without status was six years, far in excess of that required to discover all options to obtain legal status.
All these actions and inactions I find to be inconsistent with a fear of serious harm in Colombia.
Was the claimant in any way a supporter of a human rights group known as XXXXX XXXXX I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities she was not.
Not only did the claimant not mention XXXXX XXXXX by name to the Immigration Officer at the time of making her claim, she went further to state she had never belonged to any organization.
Her explanation was at this time she was under the influence of her abusive husband and she was never a member of XXXXX XXXXX only a supporter. I do not accept these explanations.
Question 5 of Schedule 12 is clear that organizations you were associated with are to be included.

If the family fled Colombia due to their support for this small group (only 35 participants) and the claimant believes her association with this group has made her a possible target of FARC then I would have expected the organization to be named or at a minimum, she should mention supporting human rights groups in XXXXX. I also reject the explanation that her husband made her sign an incorrect document. There would be no reason for her not to advance her claim separate from his. If the relationship had not dissolved they would have had two chances to gain legal status in Canada.

The only supporting document, other than the claimant's amended narrative3, is a faxed letter entered the day of the hearing4. There is no independent evidence to support such a group existed or that many of its members have been murdered. Since I do not have any cover letter or even the fax cover sheet of the faxed letter found at Exhibit C-4, I do not know how this letter was sent or from where the letter was sent. Hence I give it insufficient weight to off-set the inconsistent answer in Schedule 15.

There is no mention of XXXXX XXXXX in the first version of the Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative6. Hence this narrative does not off-set the inconsistent answer to the Immigration Officer with her latter evidence.
On a balance of probabilities the claimant did not belong or was associated with XXXXX XXXXX. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)
Is Bogota a viable IFA?
The claimant testified that if she did not fear harm from FARC or the AUC there would be no other reason she could not live in Bogota.
At the time the family was allegedly active in both the running of XXXXX and in supporting XXXXX XXXXX, the claimant was never approached or communicated to by FARC or the AUC.
According to her evidence during her return visits to Colombia she was never approached even in XXXXX by either group.
Hence I am satisfied that FARC or the AUC had no interest in the claimant in XXXXX during the period when her family was possibly being threatened.

That being the case if the claimant was to return to an area such as Bogota where she has never lived and considering she has never been targeted in XXXXX where she lived in the past, satisfies me there is little possibility of her being tracked and harmed in Bogota.
The claimant testified that other than her fear of harm there were no other reasons she could not live in Bogota. State Protection in Bogota
My analysis consists of two parts.
Part I is a review of the documentary evidence to establish that in Bogota, Colombia is making serious efforts to provide adequate protection for its citizens who fear FARC.
Part II is an analysis of the claimant's evidence provided to establish that for her these efforts would on a balance of probabilities provide inadequate protection, even in Bogota. Part I

Is the state making serious efforts to provide adequate but not necessarily perfect protection for persons similar to this claimant in Bogota today? I am satisfied for the following analysis this is the case. In my review of the documentary evidence I note: * Colombia is a constitutional democracy, * The most recent elections were generally considered fair and free and to took place in an atmosphere of freedom, transparency and normalcy.7 * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of multi-level security forces consisting of local, national police forces and a national army.8 * The National Police are responsible for internal law enforcement, shared with the Department of Administrative Security and the Prosecutor General's Corps of Technical Investigators.9
A new criminal procedure code has been in place since January 2008, resulting in shorter pretrial waiting periods and a conviction rate of 60 percent as opposed to the previous rate of 3 percent.10

The Prosecutor General's Office runs a witness protection program.11 The Prosecutor General's Office investigates criminal offenses. Its Human Rights Unit, in 13 satellite offices, specialized in investigating human rights crimes. As of December 2008, 101 specialized prosecutors were handling 4,500 cases.12 There were incidents in the past and in 2008 when elements of the security forces acted in violation of state policy, the law and or rules of engagement. Many procedures are now in place to provide recourse to the rule of law for victims, for example: * The Ministry of Defense investigated personnel suspected of collaboration with new right wing paramilitary groups culpable parties were handed over to civilian authorities. * Military or civilian authorities investigated killings committed by security forces. * Military and police accused of torture were now tried in civilian rather than the military courts. * During 2008 the Ministry of Defense relieved from duty, 80 officers and 213 NCO and soldiers for unethical conduct.13
These efforts have resulted in fewer killings by security forces in 2008 than in 2007.14

This review of the United States, Department of State, Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 200815 satisfies me that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to security forces when they require protection from criminal acts and human rights investigators for protection from human rights abuse. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law.
Historically, Colombians have feared left wing guerrillas, the FARC, the National Liberation Army (ELN) and right wing paramilitary groups such as the AUC.

Many Colombian governments in the past took steps to control the FARC and ELN with marginal success. Since 2002, the current government, with the assistance of the US, has committed significant resources to protecting its citizens from harm, from the two left wing groups.

Of particular interest in reviewing the current situation as it pertains to FARC in Colombia today, are the two reports by the International Crisis Group 4.1 from April 2008 and 4.5 from March 2009. Both are recent and all statements are fully documented. In addition, the Group is guided by well known and respected international personalities, including a former Prime Minister of Canada and an internationally recognized Canadian jurist.

The first report outlines the problems that the current Uribe government has created for FARC since 2002. * Many experienced commanders have been killed by security forces, assassinated by other insurgents, or died. This has severely disrupted communications and internal cohesion. * No Colombian political party any longer supports FARC as a legitimate left-wing force. * FARC's command structure after six years of sustained military pressure is believed to be faltering due to a lack of internal communication. * Security forces believe FARC is less operational, i.e. in 2007 there were only between 9,000 to11,000 fighters supporting FARC as opposed to approximately 19,000 in 2002, and only 10 of its former 71 fronts are currently regularly active. * The new government policy is to expand the presence of security forces in remote areas to re-establish the rule of law in these areas. * FARC units now have specialized in the use of land mines and attacks against specific police and military targets. * FARC is managing to infltrate armed force commands. * To compensate for losses, rural fronts are being reinforced with urban militia. * FARC is attemtping to regain legitimacy in the rual population by avoiding harm to civilians while focusing on high impact military targets. * The more recent 2009 report notes: * Key units of FARC have withdrawn to the jungle and mountains. * New tactics rely on ambushes. * At the tactical level, structures have decentralized; however, the Secretariat is capable of co-ordinating actions around the country. * Even though FARC has replaced its leaders in its senior command, co-ordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders is difficult. * Demobilized fighters remain in big cities to decrease the risk of being targeted by FARC. * After pushing FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries, ..., the secuity forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * Areas where FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Purumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban populations.) * Security forces fear FARC will attempt to win back status in urbans areas through terrorism. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraph of page 12 indicate FARC urban structures have been disrupted; however, insurgents remain active in Cali and Bueneventura. Now FARC work in independent cells, support networks have been progressivly weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have made logistics vulnerable to interception and exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead from combat areas. * Extortion may have increased but is under-reported. Individuals may be using FARC's name as a mean to extract extortion. * Drug revenues have dropped from one billion to 500-600 million per year. * ELN leadership has called for an alliance with FARC; however, this generally has not occurred. In areas where ELN formations have been decimated, there have been links with FARC fronts. * Section 8 (page 15) states that in urban areas FARC support has vanished. Tens of thousands marched in Bogota against FARC in March 2008. FARC continues to control remote areas. * FARC is actively working with youth in universities to again create a base of political support. * Security forces have increased to more than 400,000 in 2007 and have been successful in forcing FARC to retreat. Since 2007, security forces have expanded their presence in rural areas. * The insurgents are not close to defeat for a number of reasons; however, the government strategy aimed at a military victory is showing visible results as of 2007.

The theme of the International Crisis Group reports is reflected in the research of the Board. Item 4.3 of Exhibit R/A-116 at page 3 indicates that a news report in February 2008 reported FARC is relying on drug trafficking for its financial support since kidnapping and extortion are in decline.
In addition, the Colombian Minister of Defence indicated to the BBC that FARC currently lacks means of communication.

The United States Department of State Report for 200817 indicates FARC and ELN engage in human rights abuses, including political killings, murder of security force personnel, kidnappings, intimidation of judges, recruitment of child soldiers, and killings of teachers and trade unionists.
At page 10, the report provides specifics as to murders and abductions by FARC.

The only 2008 reference to an incident in a large urban centre occurred in September when a car bomb killed four civilians in front of a court house in XXXXX. This type of incident would not generally be considered a targeted killing. Many killings of former paramilitary were reported as well as members of security forces. (There is no evidence these occurred in Bogota.)

This review satisfies me that the State of Colombia is making serious efforts to provide adequate protection for its citizens who fear the FARC. These efforts are not always perfect but are most successful in urban areas such as Bogota. Part II

There is no evidence the claimant or her family has ever gone to the authorities for assistance. The claimant has never been threatened or harmed and hence would have had no reason to approach the government forces.
Counsel disclosed documents outlining country conditions as part of Exhibit C-2.
The XXXXX XXXXX article dated XXXXX, 2009 indicates persons trying to regain lands seized by guerrillas were killed18. The claimant's family XXXXX XXXXX.

Page 26 of Exhibit C-2 indicates FARC militia now keep a low profile and goes on to state what the documents I reviewed earlier indicate, that "the militias have not had room to maneuver because of the military and police controls but meet and recruit young people at the universities."
There is much information concerning the efforts of FARC to regroup. However, there is also much information as to the successes government forces have had in disrupting the reorganization.
There are reports of arrests and confessions of former FARC members throughout the article19.

The 2008 United Nations Report20 is included in the package. This report does not indicate that FARC is able to operate within large cities such as Bogota at a level where an individual who was of interest to the FARC in the past would be tracked and harmed.

After reviewing the claimant's evidence and counsel's disclosure, I am satisfied that the claimant has failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that for her state protection would be inadequate in Bogota. In summary -
The claimant was not targeted in the past.
The claimant's actions are inconsistent with her stated fear.
The claimant's evidence as to her support for XXXXX XXXXX was not credible.
Bogota would be both reasonable and safe for the claimant should she return to this city in Colombia. Conclusion

For all the above, I am satisfied that the claimant failed to establish there is a serious possibility she will be persecuted or suffer other forms of serious harm should she return to Colombia today.

Hence the Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act21 (IRPA).
